Unlike other major bowls, the Fiesta Bowl has not always had major conference tie-ins. For the first nine editions, the [[Western Athletic Conference]] champion was invited to the bowl. In 1997, the Fiesta Bowl agreed to invite the champion of the newly-formed [[Big 12 Conference]]; the tie-in continued until 2014 when the Big 12 moved to the [[Sugar Bowl]]. During the late 1980s, the Fiesta Bowl used its lack of tie-ins to create two ''de facto'' national championship games between [[FBS independents|independents]] or teams from conferences without mandatory bowl obligations. These games increased the Fiesta Bowl's stature. Beginning in [[1992 NCAA Division I-A football season|1992]], the Fiesta Bowl joined with several other bowls to create the [[Bowl Coalition]] in an effort to produce an [[Bowl Championship Series|undisputed national champion]] in college football. It subsequently was part of the [[Bowl Alliance]] and [[Bowl Championship Series]]. From 1992 to 2006, the Fiesta Bowl served as the national championship game of these systems in [[1996 Fiesta Bowl|1996]], [[1999 Fiesta Bowl|1999]], and [[2002 Fiesta Bowl|2002]]. The Phoenix metropolitan area and the Fiesta Bowl Committee hosted the [[BCS National Championship Game]] in [[2007 BCS National Championship Game|2007]] and [[2011 BCS National Championship Game|2011]] in addition to the regular Fiesta Bowl game. In [[2014 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2014]], the Fiesta Bowl, along with the "[[New Year's Six]]" bowls, became a part of the [[College Football Playoff]]. As part of the four team playoff from 2014 to [[2023 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2023]], the Fiesta Bowl served as a semifinal game in [[2016 Fiesta Bowl (December)|2016]], [[2019 Fiesta Bowl|2019]], and [[2022 Fiesta Bowl (December)|2022]]. With the expansion of the College Football Playoff to twelve teams in the [[2024 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2024–25 season]], the Fiesta Bowl serves as either a quarterfinal or semifinal. It was the quarterfinal for the [[2024 Fiesta Bowl (December)|2024]] season and will be the semifinal for the 2025 season. While a semifinal, the game will be played one week after New Year's Day.{{Cite web |title=About the 12-Team College Football Playoff Format |url=https://collegefootballplayoff.com/sports/2024/5/29/12-team-format.aspx |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=College Football Playoff |language=en}} The Fiesta Bowl has donated over $12 million to charity.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/national-sports/sns-he-runs-one-amateur-football-game-per-year-he-makes-more-than-1-million-20181226-story.html|title=He runs one amateur football game per year. He makes more than $1 million - NY Daily News|last=Hobson|first=Will|newspaper=New York Daily News|access-date=2018-12-30}} In 2020, it donated $1 million in emergency relief during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].{{Cite web|last=Harker|first=Victoria|date=2020-04-21|title=Most charitable bowl in nation focuses on youth programs during COVID-19|url=https://chamberbusinessnews.com/2020/04/21/most-charitable-bowl-in-nation-focuses-on-youth-programs-during-covid-19/|access-date=2020-07-23|website=Chamber Business News|language=en-US}} The current public address announcer of the Fiesta Bowl, as well as State Farm Stadium, is Jim Barnett, who has also served as pregame announcer for the three [[Super Bowl]]s played at the stadium and was the announcer of the [[2015 Pro Bowl]]. ==History== {{more citations needed section|date=April 2016}} ===Origins=== [[File:Fiesta Bowl unsponsored logo.svg|thumb|200px|right|Fiesta Bowl logo with no corporate sponsor]] The Fiesta Bowl was born from the [[Western Athletic Conference]]'s frustrated attempts to obtain bowl invitations for its champions. In [[1968 NCAA University Division football season|1968]] and [[1969 NCAA University Division football season|1969]] respectively, champions [[Wyoming Cowboys football|Wyoming]] and [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State]] failed to secure any bowl selection. The [[1970 NCAA University Division football season|next year]], undefeated Arizona State was bypassed by the major bowls and had to settle for an appearance in the less prestigious [[Peach Bowl]]. The Fiesta Bowl therefore initially provided an automatic berth for the WAC champion. ===1970s=== In its first decade of existence, the Fiesta Bowl was played in the last week of December (including the afternoon of [[Christmas Day]] from 1976 to 1979). The 1971 inaugural game featured another top-ten Arizona State squad against top-twenty opponent [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State]]. The 1974 game featured WAC champ [[BYU Cougars football|BYU]] and their new coach, future Hall of Fame member [[LaVell Edwards]] in their first-ever bowl game vs. Oklahoma State. BYU was in control until BYU's first All-American quarterback [[Gary Sheide]] went down with a leg injury and eventually lost 16–6. By 1975, the game was able to attract [[Big Eight Conference|Big Eight]] co-champion [[1975 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|Nebraska]] to play undefeated Arizona State in a matchup of top-five teams. In 1977, the game was again able to attract a top-five opponent in [[1977 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|Penn State]], despite WAC champion #16 [[BYU Cougars football|BYU]] refusing to play in the bowl due to its being held on Sunday. In 1978, [[Arizona Wildcats football|Arizona]] and Arizona State both joined the [[Pacific-10 Conference|Pac-10 Conference]] and the Fiesta Bowl's tie-in with the WAC ended, so its champ went to the newly inaugurated [[Holiday Bowl]]. From then until the advent of the [[Bowl Coalition]] in 1992, Fiesta Bowl matchups typically featured runners-up of major conferences and/or major independents. ===1980s=== The game continued to attract high quality matchups. Beginning with the [[1982 Fiesta Bowl|1981]] season, it shifted to [[New Year's Day]] alongside the major bowl games—the [[1982 Cotton Bowl Classic|Cotton]], [[1982 Orange Bowl|Orange]], [[1982 Sugar Bowl|Sugar]], and [[1982 Rose Bowl|Rose]]. At the time, [[NBC Sports|NBC]] had the broadcast rights to the Fiesta, Rose, and Orange; the Fiesta was played first and had a late morning kickoff (11:30 a.m. [[Mountain Time Zone|MST]]). It was the first bowl game to acquire a corporate [[Naming rights|title sponsor]], via an agreement with [[Sunkist Growers]] in September 1985, making the game the "Sunkist Fiesta Bowl" starting with the [[1986 Fiesta Bowl|January 1986 edition]].{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/65966770/sunkist-agrees-to-sponsor-fiesta-bowl/ |title=Sunkist agrees to sponsor Fiesta Bowl |first=Bob |last=Young |newspaper=[[The Arizona Republic]] |location=[[Phoenix, Arizona]] |page=G1 |date=September 27, 1985 |access-date=December 24, 2020 |via=newspapers.com}}{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/65967219/sunkist-agrees-to-sponsor-fiesta-bowl/ |title=Sunkist agrees to sponsor Fiesta Bowl (cont'd) |first=Bob |last=Young |newspaper=[[The Arizona Republic]] |location=[[Phoenix, Arizona]] |page=G3 |date=September 27, 1985 |access-date=December 24, 2020 |via=newspapers.com}} The [[Tangerine Bowl (1947–1982)|Tangerine Bowl]] had previously reached agreement in March 1983 with the Florida Citrus Commission, a state government agency, to rename itself as the Florida Citrus Bowl.{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/65962888/1-million-citrus-bowl-approved/ |title=$1 million Citrus Bowl approved |first=Dan |last=Tracy |newspaper=[[Orlando Sentinel]] |page=C1 |date=March 17, 1983 |access-date=December 24, 2020 |via=newspapers.com}} A major breakthrough occurred after the [[1986 NCAA Division I-A football season|1986]] season when the top two teams in the country, [[1986 Miami Hurricanes football team|Miami]] and [[1986 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|Penn State]], agreed to play for the ''de facto'' [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championship]] in the Fiesta Bowl. At the time, the traditional four "major" bowl games granted automatic bids to their conference champions. Both Miami and Penn State were [[NCAA Division I FBS independent schools|independents]] at that time, and were thus free to choose a bowl. As such, the Fiesta Bowl and the [[Citrus Bowl (game)|Florida Citrus Bowl]], each free from the obligation of conference tie-ins, vied to host the Miami–Penn State matchup in order to ensure that they would meet on the field. The Fiesta Bowl won the bidding and [[1987 Fiesta Bowl|the game]] was set to be played on Friday, January 2, 1987—the night after the "big four" bowls of New Year's Day. Penn State won {{nowrap|14–10,}} and the game drew the largest television audience in the history of college football at the time. Two years later, #1 [[1988 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]] played undefeated #3 [[1988 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|West Virginia]] for the national championship at the [[1989 Fiesta Bowl]] on January 1. The 1987 and 1989 games were two of four straight matchups of teams ranked in the AP Top 10 going into the bowl season to close out the 1980s. This significantly increased the Fiesta Bowl's prestige, to the point that it was now considered a major bowl by many fans and pundits. The [[1988 Fiesta Bowl|1988]] game returned to New Year's Day, and the 1989 game kicked off three hours later (2:30 p.m. MST on NBC) and opposite the [[1989 Rose Bowl|Rose Bowl]], which had switched networks to [[ESPN College Football on ABC|ABC]]. ===1990s=== Before the [[1991 Fiesta Bowl|1991 game]], several major universities declined invitations due to the [[Arizona|State of Arizona's]] decision at that time not to adopt the [[Martin Luther King, Jr. Day|Martin Luther King Holiday]]. However, in [[1992 NCAA Division I-A football season|1992]], the Fiesta Bowl was invited to participate in the [[Bowl Coalition]], a predecessor to the [[Bowl Championship Series]]. This assured the game would feature major conference champions or prestigious runners-up and cemented its status as a major bowl. Had the two top-ranked teams in the Bowl Coalition not come from the SEC, Big Eight or SWC, the Fiesta Bowl would have hosted the Bowl Coalition's "national championship game," though this never happened during the three years of the Bowl Coalition's run. When the Bowl Coalition was reconfigured as the [[Bowl Alliance]] for the 1995 season, the Fiesta was included as one of the three top games. [[1996 Fiesta Bowl|In that season]], it hosted the Bowl Alliance National Championship game featuring undefeated #1 [[1995 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|Nebraska]] playing undefeated #2 [[1995 Florida Gators football team|Florida]] for the national championship. Nebraska won the game 62–24, the largest win margin in the history of the national championship game, and the most points ever scored in a national championship game. Finally, with the addition of the [[Big Ten Conference|Big Ten]] and [[Pacific-10 Conference|Pac-10]] conferences to the new [[Bowl Championship Series]], the Fiesta Bowl became a permanent fixture in the four-year [[BCS National Championship Game]] rotation. In [[1998 NCAA Division I-A football season|1998]], the Fiesta Bowl featured the first [[1999 BCS National Championship Game|BCS National Championship Game]], which [[1998 Tennessee Volunteers football team|Tennessee]] won over Florida State, 23–16. Starting with the 1999 season, the [[Big 12 Conference]] champion received an automatic bid to the Fiesta Bowl in years when it was not slated as the BCS title game, an arrangement that continued to the end of the BCS era. ===2000s=== [[File:Fiesta Bowl 2006 from Flickr 81639095.jpg|thumb|right|2006 Fiesta Bowl, the last Fiesta Bowl game in Sun Devil Stadium]] In [[2001 NCAA Division I-A football season|2002]], the [[2002 Fiesta Bowl|Fiesta Bowl]] had the right to take the Pac-10 Conference Champion, should that team not reach the [[2002 Rose Bowl|Rose Bowl]], which served as the national championship game that season. Oregon failed to qualify for the championship game, and thus played Colorado in the Fiesta Bowl. A similar arrangement was made for the [[2006 Fiesta Bowl]]. However, instead of gaining the Pac-10 Conference champion in addition to their usual tie-in with the Big 12, the Fiesta Bowl would have had a choice of the two teams. This turned out to be a moot point as both the Big 12 champion [[2005 Texas Longhorns football team|Texas]] and Pac-10 champion [[2005 USC Trojans football team|Southern California]] qualified for the National Championship Game (USC's participation has since been vacated). {{cite news| url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20011117/oregon18/oregon-clinches-berth-in-fiesta-bowl-national-title-still-a-possibility | work=The Seattle Times | title=Oregon clinches berth in Fiesta Bowl; National title still a possibility | date=November 17, 2001}} [[File:Adrian Peterson OUvsBSU.jpg|thumb|right|2007 Fiesta Bowl, Boise State vs. Oklahoma; January 1, 2007, the first Fiesta Bowl at University of Phoenix Stadium]] The BCS National Championship game returned to the [[2003 Fiesta Bowl|Fiesta Bowl]] in [[2002 NCAA Division I-A football season|2003]] with the Big Ten champions [[2002 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|Ohio State Buckeyes]] beating the Big East champions [[2002 Miami Hurricanes football team|Miami Hurricanes]] in the first overtime national championship game. The game went into double overtime with the Buckeyes coming out on top 31–24 to claim the 2002 national championship. The Fiesta Bowl was the first [[BCS bowl]] to have had a team from outside the automatic qualifying (AQ) BCS conferences (the [[Big 12 Conference|Big 12]], [[Big Ten Conference|Big Ten]], [[Atlantic Coast Conference]] (ACC), [[Southeastern Conference]] (SEC), [[Pacific-10 Conference|Pac-10]], [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East]], and [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]]). The [[2005 Fiesta Bowl|2005 game]] saw undefeated [[2004 Utah Utes football team|Utah]] from the [[Mountain West Conference]] become the first BCS non-AQ school ever to play in a BCS game, easily defeating [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East]] champion [[2004 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|Pittsburgh]] 35–7. In [[2006 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2007]], the Fiesta Bowl game was played for the first time at the new then-named [[State Farm Stadium|University of Phoenix Stadium]] in [[Glendale, Arizona|Glendale]], across the [[Phoenix metropolitan area]] from Sun Devil Stadium. The undefeated [[2006 Boise State Broncos football team|Boise State Broncos]] won by defeating the [[2006 Oklahoma Sooners football team|Oklahoma Sooners]] 43–42 in [[Overtime (sports)#American and Canadian football|overtime]]. It has been called [[2007 Fiesta Bowl|one of the greatest college football games ever played]], due to the combination of an underdog team, [[trick play]]s, comebacks by each team, and a thrilling overtime finish.{{cite news| first = Pete | last = Thamel |author-link=Pete Thamel | title = Playbook Full of Tricks Gives Boise State Dramatic and Defining Victory |url = https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/02/sports/ncaafootball/02fiesta.html | work=The New York Times | date =2007-01-02 | access-date =2007-01-02}} ===2010s=== The [[2010 Fiesta Bowl]] featured #6 [[2009 Boise State Broncos football team|Boise State]] defeating #4 [[2009 TCU Horned Frogs football team|TCU]], 17–10. It was the first time a BCS bowl matched-up two non-automatic qualifying teams (i.e. two teams from conferences without automatic BCS bids) and the first time that two teams who went undefeated faced each other in a BCS game outside of the national championship. In the [[2012 Fiesta Bowl]], [[2011 Oklahoma State Cowboys football team|Oklahoma State]] defeated [[2011 Stanford Cardinal football team|Stanford]] 41–38. Notable players included [[Brandon Weeden]] and [[Justin Blackmon]] for Oklahoma State, and [[Andrew Luck]] for Stanford. In November 2016, [[PlayStation]] was announced as the bowl's new title sponsor.{{cite press release|title=Fiesta Bowl Names PlayStation as New Title Sponsor|url=https://fiestabowl.org/news-room/fiesta-bowl-names-playstation-new-title-sponsor/|website=FiestaBowl.org|date=November 15, 2016|access-date=November 16, 2016|archive-date=November 16, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116225516/https://fiestabowl.org/news-room/fiesta-bowl-names-playstation-new-title-sponsor/|url-status=dead}} The [[2016 Fiesta Bowl (December)|December 2016]], [[2019 Fiesta Bowl (December)|December 2019]], [[2022 Fiesta Bowl (December)|December 2022]], and [[2026 Fiesta Bowl|January 2026]] editions served as a semifinal for the [[College Football Playoff]]. The Fiesta Bowl is expected to next host a semifinal, alongside the [[Peach Bowl]], in January 2029. === 2020s === The [[2021 Fiesta Bowl|50th edition]] of the Fiesta Bowl featured #10 [[2020 Iowa State Cyclones football team|Iowa State]] defeating #25 [[2020 Oregon Ducks football team|Oregon Ducks]], 34–17. The game was behind closed doors due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Arizona]], with only players' family members admitted. In the [[2022 Fiesta Bowl (January)|2022 Fiesta Bowl]], [[2021 Oklahoma State Cowboys football team|Oklahoma State]] rallied from a 28–7 deficit late in the second quarter to defeat [[2021 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]], 37–35. In the [[2022 Fiesta Bowl (December)|December edition]] of that game (which was also a CFP semifinal), #3 [[2022 TCU Horned Frogs football team|TCU]] defeated #2 [[2022 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]], 51–45, the highest scoring game in Fiesta Bowl history, and the second-highest scoring CFP semifinal game. In the [[2026 Fiesta Bowl (January)|2026 Fiesta Bowl]], the tenth–ranked [[2025 Miami Hurricanes football team|Miami Hurricanes]] upset the sixth–ranked [[2025 Ole Miss Rebels football team|Ole Miss Rebels]], 31–27, in the CFP semifinals. ==Controversies== ===Invitations=== In 1996, a group of students from [[Brigham Young University]], led by BYU professor Dennis Martin, burned bags of Tostitos tortilla chips in a bonfire and called for a boycott of all Tostitos products.[http://starbulletin.com/96/12/11/sports/notebook.html 1996 AP archives] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071112154716/http://starbulletin.com/96/12/11/sports/notebook.html |date=2007-11-12 }}. the weeks prior to the 2010 Fiesta Bowl, past and present Fiesta Bowl employees alleged that they were encouraged to help maintain its position as one of the four [[Bowl Championship Series|BCS bowls]] by making campaign contributions to politicians friendly to the Fiesta Bowl, with those contributions subsequently reimbursed to the employees. If the allegations were true, this would have been a violation of both state and federal campaign finance laws.{{cite web|url=http://www.azcentral.com/arizonarepublic/news/articles/2009/12/18/20091218fiesta-bowl-investigation.html|title=Fiesta Bowl employees say bowl repaid political contributions}} Furthermore, as a non-profit organization, the Fiesta Bowl is prohibited from making political contributions of any kind.{{cite web|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/314585-fiesta-bowl-scandal-causes-stir|title=Fiesta Bowl Scandal Causes Stir|website=[[Bleacher Report]] }} The Fiesta Bowl commissioned an "independent review" which found "no credible evidence that the bowl's management engaged in any type of illegal or unethical conduct."{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/blogs/blog-briefing-room/news/57598-fiesta-bowl-finds-no-wrongdoing-after-allegations-of-illegal-political-donations/|title=Fiesta Bowl finds no wrongdoing after allegations of illegal political donations|date=24 December 2009 }} The following year, in a November 2010 article, ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' reported that Fiesta Bowl officials, including bowl CEO John Junker, had spent $4 million since 2000 to curry favor from BCS bigwigs and elected officials, including a 2008 "Fiesta Frolic", a golf-centered gathering of athletic directors and head coaches. The journal also reported that Junker's annual salary was close to $600,000 and that the bowl in 2007 turned an $11.6 million profit.Murphy, Austin, and Dan Wetzel, "Does It Matter?", ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'', 15 November 2010, p. 45. While these alleged activities are not illegal, they did result in considerable damage to the reputation of the Fiesta Bowl. On March 29, 2011, the Fiesta Bowl Board of Directors released a 276-page "scathing internal report", commissioned by them to re-examine the accusations of illegal political activities.{{cite web|url=http://www.fiestabowl.org/_documents/reports/Fiesta_Bowl_Final_Public.pdf|title=Final Report|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110511190532/http://www.fiestabowl.org/_documents/reports/Fiesta_Bowl_Final_Public.pdf|archive-date=2011-05-11}} The commission determined that $46,539 of illegal campaign contributions were made and the board immediately fired Fiesta Bowl CEO John Junker, who had already been suspended pending the results of this investigation.{{Cite news |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=6270459 |title=Fiesta Bowl fires CEO John Junker |date=March 29, 2011 |agency=Associated Press}} The scandal threatened the Fiesta Bowl's status as a BCS game, as the BCS said it might replace the bowl in its lineup if officials could not convince them it should remain.{{cite web|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/football/ncaa/03/30/fiesta-bowl-bcs.ap/index.html#ixzz1I8IZ4dwj|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110403014431/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2011/football/ncaa/03/30/fiesta-bowl-bcs.ap/index.html#ixzz1I8IZ4dwj|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 3, 2011|title=BCS confident it could cut ties with Fiesta Bowl if deemed necessary}}Wetzel, Dan, "[https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/news?slug=dw-wetzel_bcs_fiesta_bowl_ceo_money_scheme033011 BCS conducts shallow probe as party rages on]", ''Yahoo! Sports'', retrieved on 31 March 2011. The BCS ultimately chose not to expel the Fiesta Bowl, instead fining the organization $1 million. In June 2011 [[University of Arizona]] president Robert Shelton was hired to replace Junker.[[Associated Press]], "Fiesta Bowl names new president", ''[[Japan Times]]'', 15 June 2011, p. 15.
